# Point source, point detector {#sec-point-source}

This chapter solves @eq-rte of @sec-rte for a single point source and a
single point isotropic detector in an infinite, homogeneous medium, at one
wavelength $\lambda$. It is the exact math behind `src/lighthit`; every
boxed result is cross-referenced to the function that implements it.

The route from @eq-rte to code has four steps, in this order: a space–time
Fourier transform turns the streaming PDE into an algebraic equation, one
$\mathbf k$ at a time (@sec-fourier); reciprocity trades "solve once for
every source direction" for "solve once, evaluate anywhere" (@sec-adjoint);
expanding the remaining angular dependence in Legendre polynomials, with
the polar axis along $\mathbf k$, turns that one solve into an exact,
tridiagonal linear system (@sec-matrix) — @sec-method-choice explains why
this, rather than a direct real-space spherical-harmonic expansion; and an
inverse Fourier–Bessel transform brings the result back to $(\mathbf r,t)$
(@sec-spatial, @sec-coordinate-first, @sec-charge). Keep this chain in mind
throughout: every symbol introduced below is a waypoint on it, not a new
unrelated quantity.

## Setup and normalization {#sec-setup}

The medium is infinite and homogeneous. Absorption $\mu_a>0$ and scattering
$\mu_s\ge0$ are in $\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\mu_t=\mu_a+\mu_s$, and the group speed
$v=c_0/n_g$ is in m/ns with $c_0=0.299792458$ m/ns. Polarization, wavelength
change on scattering, refracting boundaries, and reflections are not
included. $I(\mathbf x,\mathbf s,t)$ is the intensity of @sec-rte, and the
transport equation reads
$$
\left(\frac1v\partial_t+\mathbf s\cdot\nabla+\mu_t\right)I
-\mu_s\int p(\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf s')I(\mathbf s')\,\mathrm d\Omega'
=q.
$$ {#eq-rte-local}

A directed single-photon flash at $t=0$ is
$$q=\delta^3(\mathbf x)\,\delta(t)\,\delta_{S^2}(\mathbf s-\mathbf s_0),$$
with $q$ integrating to one photon over space, time, and direction. For an
isotropic flash the angular delta function is replaced by $1/(4\pi)$.

An ideal detector measures the scalar flux
$$K(\mathbf r,t;\mathbf s_0)=\int I(\mathbf r,\mathbf s,t)\,\mathrm d\Omega,$$
the response **per unit effective area**, in $\mathrm m^{-2}\,\mathrm{ns}^{-1}$.
This is not the same as the signed vector flux $\int\mathbf sI\,\mathrm d\Omega$
through a plane. The detector's angular sensitivity is isotropic and its
efficiency is 1; the expected count of a small detector of area $A$ is
$A\int K\,\mathrm dt$. The radius or shape of a finite optical module (OM)
is not modeled yet.

For the directed flash,
$$K^{(0)}(\mathbf r,t;\mathbf s_0)=v\,e^{-\mu_tvt}\,\delta^3(\mathbf r-vt\,\mathbf s_0),\qquad t>0,$$ {#eq-k0-directed}
a single spike travelling outward along $\mathbf s_0$ at speed $v$. On the
exact forward ray this has no finite pointwise value; the API rejects that
request (see `PointGreenSolver.solve`). In every other direction $K^{(0)}=0$.
For the isotropic flash,
$$K^{(0)}(r,t)=\frac{e^{-\mu_tr}}{4\pi r^2}\,\delta(t-r/v),\qquad r>0,$$ {#eq-k0-iso}
whose integral over a time bin is computed in closed form (@sec-charge).
Both are derived from scratch in @sec-ballistic, together with the tool the
rest of the chapter reuses.

## The Fourier transport equation {#sec-fourier}

For any field $u(\mathbf x,t)$, define its space–time Fourier transform
$$
\tilde u(\mathbf k,\omega)=\int \mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm dt\ u(\mathbf x,t)\,
e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x+i\omega t},
$$ {#eq-fourier-def}
with $\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\omega$ in $\mathrm{rad/ns}$. A tilde
marks this transform **everywhere** in this book. A hat over a unit vector,
as in $\widehat{\mathbf k}=\mathbf k/k$ or $\widehat{\mathbf r}=\mathbf r/r$,
is unrelated to it — it just means "divide by the length" — and never
denotes a transform.

Under @eq-fourier-def, integrating by parts and dropping boundary terms at
spatial and temporal infinity gives $\partial_t\to-i\omega$ and
$\nabla\to i\mathbf k$. The scattering integral in @eq-rte-local does not
touch $\mathbf x$ or $t$, so it transforms termwise, into an operator $V$
acting only on the direction $\mathbf s$:
$$
(V u)(\mathbf s):=\mu_s\int p(\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf s')\,u(\mathbf s')\,
\mathrm d\Omega'.
$$
Collecting every term of @eq-rte-local,
$$
\boxed{(D-V)\tilde I=\tilde q,}\qquad
D(\mathbf s)=d_0+ik\mu,\quad d_0=\mu_t-i\omega/v,
\quad k=|\mathbf k|,\quad \mu=\widehat{\mathbf k}\cdot\mathbf s.
$$ {#eq-master}
This holds **per $\mathbf k$**: different wavenumbers never mix, because
the medium's homogeneity is exactly what a Fourier transform in $\mathbf x$
diagonalizes (@sec-method-choice returns to why that matters). $\mathrm{Re}(d_0)=\mu_t>0$
makes $D-V$ invertible for every real $\omega$ and every physical medium; that
positivity is what selects the causal, retarded solution automatically, with
no separate initial condition to impose by hand. @eq-master is the equation
solved, in one form or another, for the rest of this chapter — everything
that follows is either a special case of it (@sec-ballistic), a reformulation
of what to do with it (@sec-adjoint), or an inversion of its solution back
to $(\mathbf r,t)$ (@sec-spatial onward).

## Deriving the ballistic term {#sec-ballistic}

Set $V=0$ in @eq-master — no scattering — with the directed-flash source. Its
Fourier transform is
$$
\tilde q(\mathbf k,\mathbf s,\omega)=\int\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm dt\,
\delta^3(\mathbf x)\delta(t)\delta_{S^2}(\mathbf s-\mathbf s_0)\,
e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x+i\omega t}=\delta_{S^2}(\mathbf s-\mathbf s_0),
$$
independent of $\mathbf k,\omega$: the space and time deltas simply evaluate
the exponential at the origin. @eq-master then reads $D(\mathbf s)\tilde I(\mathbf s)
=\delta(\mathbf s-\mathbf s_0)$, and since $D$ is an ordinary, nonzero
multiplier (no integral operator left to invert), the solution is itself a
delta, scaled by $D$ at the point it sits on:
$$
\tilde I^{(0)}(\mathbf s)=\frac{\delta_{S^2}(\mathbf s-\mathbf s_0)}{D(\mathbf s_0)}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\tilde K^{(0)}(\mathbf k,\omega;\mathbf s_0)=\int\tilde I^{(0)}\,\mathrm d\Omega
=\frac1{D(\mathbf s_0)}.
$$ {#eq-k0-transform}
No scattering means the photon direction never leaves $\mathbf s_0$, and
@eq-k0-transform says exactly that in transform space: the whole angular
dependence stays a single spike. Everything downstream of $\mathbf s_0$ in
this chapter is this same object with $V$ turned back on.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="From 1/D(s0) back to (r,t): verifying eq-k0-directed"}
Rather than inverting a four-dimensional distributional integral from
scratch, check @eq-k0-directed by transforming it forward and confirming it
reproduces @eq-k0-transform — a short, self-contained calculation. With
$\theta$ the step function,
$$
\int\mathrm d^3r\,\mathrm dt\ v\,\theta(t)e^{-\mu_tvt}\,
\delta^3(\mathbf r-vt\mathbf s_0)\ e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r+i\omega t}
=v\int_0^\infty\mathrm dt\ e^{-\mu_tvt-ivt(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf s_0)+i\omega t}
=\frac{v}{\mu_tv+iv(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf s_0)-i\omega}
=\frac1{d_0+ik\mu},
$$
using $\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf s_0=k\mu$ with $\mu=\widehat{\mathbf k}\cdot\mathbf s_0$
in the last step — exactly $1/D(\mathbf s_0)$. $\mu_t>0$ makes the time
integral converge, which is the same positivity that made $D$ invertible
above; the two are the same causality statement.

For the isotropic flash, average @eq-k0-directed over $\mathbf s_0$ with
weight $1/(4\pi)$. Only $\mathbf s_0$ multiplies $vt$ inside the delta, so
use $\int_{S^2}\delta^3(\mathbf x-R\widehat{\mathbf s})\,\mathrm d\Omega_{\widehat{\mathbf s}}
=\delta(|\mathbf x|-R)/R^2$ with $R=vt$, $\mathbf x=\mathbf r$:
$$
K^{(0)}_{\mathrm{iso}}(r,t)=\frac{v\,e^{-\mu_tvt}}{4\pi}\cdot
\frac{\delta(r-vt)}{(vt)^2}=\frac{e^{-\mu_tr}}{4\pi r^2}\,\delta(t-r/v),
$$
using $\delta(r-vt)=\delta(t-r/v)/v$ in the last step — @eq-k0-iso.
:::

## Reciprocity: one solve for every source direction {#sec-adjoint}

Solving @eq-master directly for the directed flash means finding the
Green's function $G(\mathbf s,\mathbf s_0)$ of $L:=D-V$ on the sphere, one
$\mathbf s_0$ at a time, and then integrating it over the *output* variable,
$\tilde K(\mathbf k,\omega;\mathbf s_0)=\int G(\mathbf s,\mathbf s_0)\,
\mathrm d\Omega_{\mathbf s}$ — a fresh solve for every source direction of
interest. Reciprocity removes that per-$\mathbf s_0$ cost.

Use the bilinear pairing $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{S^2}f(\mathbf s)g(\mathbf s)\,
\mathrm d\Omega$ — no complex conjugation; this is the transport-theory
reciprocity pairing, not the Hermitian inner product, and it is what lets
the argument below go through without ever conjugating the complex $D$.
$D$ multiplies pointwise, so $\langle f,Dg\rangle=\langle Df,g\rangle$ for
*any* complex-valued $D(\mathbf s)$, trivially. $V$'s kernel $\mu_sp(\mathbf s\cdot
\mathbf s')$ depends on the dot product alone, so it is symmetric under
$\mathbf s\leftrightarrow\mathbf s'$ — true of every physical phase
function, HG included — and relabeling the dummy variable in $\langle f,Vg
\rangle$ gives $\langle f,Vg\rangle=\langle Vf,g\rangle$ too. So
$$
\langle f,Lg\rangle=\langle Lf,g\rangle\quad\text{for all }f,g,
$$
using only the **symmetry** of the phase function — nothing about it being
real-valued is needed. Now evaluate what is wanted, $\tilde K(\mathbf s_0)=
\langle1,G(\cdot,\mathbf s_0)\rangle$ with $G(\cdot,\mathbf s_0)=L^{-1}
\delta(\cdot-\mathbf s_0)$:
$$
\tilde K(\mathbf k,\omega;\mathbf s_0)
=\langle1,L^{-1}\delta(\cdot-\mathbf s_0)\rangle
=\langle L^{-1}1,\delta(\cdot-\mathbf s_0)\rangle
=\bigl[L^{-1}1\bigr](\mathbf s_0),
$$
where the middle step applies the same symmetry to $L^{-1}$ (transposes of
inverses are inverses of transposes), and the last step uses
$\langle u,\delta(\cdot-\mathbf s_0)\rangle=u(\mathbf s_0)$. Writing
$h:=L^{-1}1$ — the response to a **unit, uniform** right-hand side, not to
any particular $\mathbf s_0$ —
$$
\boxed{(D-V)h=1,}\qquad
\boxed{\tilde K(\mathbf k,\omega;\mathbf s_0)=h(\mathbf s_0).}
$$ {#eq-adjoint-h}
This is the payoff: $h$ does not know about $\mathbf s_0$ at all while it is
being solved for; $\mathbf s_0$ only enters afterward, as the point at which
the already-computed $h$ is evaluated. One tridiagonal solve per $(\mathbf
k,\omega)$ (@sec-matrix) answers the detector-response question for every
source direction at once. $h$'s meaning is now explicit and never has to be
taken on faith again: **$h(\mathbf s_0)$ is $\tilde K$, the transform of the
actual measured response**, not an auxiliary field with no direct physical
reading — @sec-spatial and @sec-charge only have left to invert it back to
$(\mathbf r,t)$. For an isotropic flash the same argument with $\tilde q=
1/(4\pi)$ in place of $\delta(\cdot-\mathbf s_0)$ gives
$\tilde K_{\mathrm{iso}}=\langle h,1/(4\pi)\rangle$, the average of $h$ over
the sphere — used from @sec-spatial on.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The Hermitian route, for comparison"}
Transport texts often build the adjoint with the Hermitian inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int f^*g\,\mathrm d\Omega$ instead. That route needs
$D^*$, produces a field $\psi$ solving $(D^*-V)\psi=1$, and recovers the
wanted quantity by a final conjugation, $h=\psi^*$. It agrees with
@eq-adjoint-h — the HG kernel is both real and symmetric, so nothing here
contradicts that derivation — but it needs the kernel's *reality* as well as
its symmetry, and reaches the boxed result in two steps instead of one. This
book uses the bilinear route throughout; `angular.py`'s `h` is exactly the
$h$ of @eq-adjoint-h, with no leftover conjugation anywhere in the code.
:::

## Why Fourier space and Legendre polynomials {#sec-method-choice}

@eq-adjoint-h is already a spherical-harmonic expansion — just not the one a
first guess might reach for, expanding $I(\mathbf x,\mathbf s,t)$ directly in
$\mathbf x$-space. Two choices explain the difference, both visible directly
in `angular.py`.

**Fourier in $\mathbf x$ first.** A direct real-space spherical-harmonic (or
discrete-ordinate) expansion still leaves $\nabla$ coupling every spatial
point to its neighbors: the angular truncation alone does not remove the
need to discretize $\mathbf x$, and a finite grid or mesh adds its own
truncation error — numerical dispersion, a chosen spacing — on top of the
angular one. The medium here is infinite and homogeneous, so translations
in $\mathbf x$ are an exact symmetry of @eq-rte-local, and the Fourier
transform diagonalizes them: @eq-master holds **per $\mathbf k$**, with zero
coupling between different $\mathbf k$. That is what removes $\mathbf x$
from the problem entirely. The only discretizations anywhere in this
chapter are the angular truncation $L$ (@sec-matrix) and the numerical $k$
quadrature (@sec-spatial) — never a spatial grid.

**Legendre, not a general $Y_{lm}$ expansion.** Once in $\mathbf k$-space,
$D(\mathbf s)=d_0+ik\mu$ depends on $\mathbf s$ only through $\mu=
\widehat{\mathbf k}\cdot\mathbf s$, the cosine to the *particular* $\mathbf
k$ being solved for. Choosing the polar axis along $\mathbf k$ — a free
choice, made independently at every $\mathbf k$ — makes $D$, and the
uniform source $1$, both invariant under rotation about that axis, so only
$m=0$ survives: the Legendre polynomials $P_l(\mu)$, not a full $(l,m)$
spherical-harmonic system. A source or phase function that was *not*
axisymmetric about $\mathbf k$ would force every $m$ back in. Streaming
couples adjacent $l$ only, by the ordinary 3-term recursion $\mu p_l=a_lp_{l-1}
+a_{l+1}p_{l+1}$ — hence tridiagonal. Scattering is **diagonal** in $l$,
with eigenvalue $\gamma_l=\mu_sg^l$, specifically because the
Henyey–Greenstein phase function's own Legendre expansion is
$p_{\mathrm{HG}}(\cos\Theta)=\sum_l\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}g^lP_l(\cos\Theta)$ — a
classical property of HG (Henyey & Greenstein 1941), not of phase functions
in general. A tabulated or otherwise non-HG phase function would still
reduce to this $m=0$, $l$-indexed problem by the same rotation argument, but
its $\Gamma$ would no longer be diagonal — `dense_finite_rank_reference`
(@sec-orders) solves exactly that more general, dense-matrix case, and is
the fallback this design keeps available.

**Reciprocity removes the last multiplicity.** @sec-adjoint's construction
means the single tridiagonal solve at each $(\mathbf k,\omega)$ — sourced by
$1$, not by $\mathbf s_0$ — already answers the question for every source
direction, and @sec-spatial folds in every observation point $\mathbf r$
afterward, algebraically, from that same $h$.

Put together: an exact, per-$\mathbf k$ algebraic system, tridiagonal
because of the streaming recursion, diagonal in its scattering part because
of HG's own Legendre expansion, solved once per $(\mathbf k,\omega)$
regardless of how many source directions or detector positions are asked
for. The only approximations left are the truncation degree $L$
(@sec-matrix) and the numerical $k,\omega$ quadratures (@sec-spatial,
@sec-charge) — never a discretization of $\mathbf x$.

## Matrix form and the exact free tail {#sec-matrix}

The HG phase function is normalized to one over the full sphere,
$$p_{\mathrm{HG}}(x)=\frac{1-g^2}{4\pi(1+g^2-2gx)^{3/2}}.$$
$g$ is a model input here, not inferred from either optical coefficient
(the private-water adapter's own default is discussed in @sec-bgvd-water).
The multiply-scattered part of the code uses the truncated operator
$$\gamma_l=\begin{cases}\mu_sg^l,&l\le L,\\0,&l>L,\end{cases}$$
where $L$ is the **scattering degree** — a truncation of the operator's
angular rank, not of the number of collisions summed (@sec-orders makes
that distinction precise). Multiplication by $\mu$ is tridiagonal in the
normalized-Legendre basis $p_l(\mu)=\sqrt{(2l+1)/2}\,P_l(\mu)$,
$$\mu p_l=a_lp_{l-1}+a_{l+1}p_{l+1},\qquad
a_l=\frac{l}{\sqrt{4l^2-1}}\ (l\ge1),\quad a_0=0,$$
so, writing $h(\mu)=\sum_lh_lp_l(\mu)$, the angular equation @eq-adjoint-h
becomes
$$\boxed{
(d_0-\gamma_l)h_l+ik\,a_lh_{l-1}+ik\,a_{l+1}h_{l+1}
=\sqrt2\,\delta_{l0}.
}$$
This is still an infinite system. Above degree $L$ its coefficients belong
to **free** transport alone. Its exact moments,
$$b_l=\int_{-1}^1\frac{p_l(\mu)}{d_0+ik\mu}\,\mathrm d\mu,$$
satisfy the same homogeneous recursion for $l>0$ — these are exactly the
Legendre coefficients of $h^{(0)}=1/D$ from @sec-ballistic, restricted to
$V=0$. Let $N\ge L$ be the last degree kept explicitly. Then, for a
right-hand side that vanishes above $L$, the free tail obeys
$$h_{N+1}=r_Nh_N,\qquad r_N=\frac{b_{N+1}}{b_N}$$
(with $r_N=0$ at $k=0$), and the code never divides small $b_l$ by one
another directly — see the collapsed derivation below for how $r_N$ is
actually computed.
The last diagonal entry of the finite matrix becomes
$$A_{NN}=d_0-\gamma_N+ik\,a_{N+1}r_N,$$
and for the remaining rows
$$A_{ll}=d_0-\gamma_l,\quad
A_{l,l-1}=ik\,a_l,\quad A_{l,l+1}=ik\,a_{l+1}.$$
This eliminates the infinite **free** tail exactly; the condition
$h_{N+1}=0$ is never imposed. A regression test moves the elimination
degree $N$ from 20 to 90 at fixed $L$ and checks that the retained
low-degree coefficients do not move.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How the tail ratio r_N is computed"}
Let $F_l=\int P_l(\mu)/(d_0+ik\mu)\,\mathrm d\mu$ and $z=id_0/k$. Then
$$
F_0=\frac2k\arctan(k/d_0),\qquad
F_1=zF_0+\frac2{ik},\qquad
F_{l+1}=\frac{(2l+1)zF_l-lF_{l-1}}{l+1}.
$$
Forward recursion in $F_l$ is used when it stays numerically safe; the
alternative is the ratio $R_l=F_{l+1}/F_l$, obtained by backward recursion,
$$
R_{l-1}=\frac{l}{(2l+1)z-(l+1)R_l},
$$
selecting the branch that decays with $l$ — the physically decaying free
solution, not the growing one that backward recursion would otherwise pick
up numerically. The normalized tail ratio is then
$r_N=\sqrt{(2N+3)/(2N+1)}\,R_N$. At $k=0$: $b_0=\sqrt2/d_0$, $b_{l>0}=0$.
Both branches are implemented in `angular.py` as `free_moments_and_tail` /
`_free_moments_and_ratios`, which switches between the forward and backward
form depending on how much the free solution has already decayed — that is
the `forward` mask built from `eta` in the source. How far the backward
recursion has to run before it is trusted is exactly the cost driver
profiled in @sec-spatial's closing note.
:::

## Separating the first orders {#sec-orders}

To avoid inverting the ballistic singularities in space, and to avoid
subtracting two nearly equal numbers, the code solves three systems built
from the **same** matrix structure instead of one:
$$
h^{(0)}=b,\qquad
A_0h^{(1)}=\Gamma b,\qquad
A_Lh^{(\ge2)}=\Gamma h^{(1)}.
$$
$\Gamma$ is the diagonal matrix of $\gamma_l$; $A_0$ contains free transport
only, and $A_L=A_0-\Gamma$. Both matrices share the same exact free tail.
The last solve sums **all** orders $2,3,\dots$ — there is no truncation of
the Neumann series in the number of collisions, only the angular truncation
at $L$ described above. For each $(k,\omega)$ this means two tridiagonal
solves, each $O(N)$, batched over every $k$ node at once (`angular_components`).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Independent check: dense matrix reference"}
`dense_finite_rank_reference` builds
$$
B_{ij}=\int_{-1}^1\frac{p_i(\mu)p_j(\mu)}{D(\mu)}\,\mathrm d\mu,
$$
solves $(1-\Gamma B)a=\Gamma b$ by ordinary dense linear algebra, and
projects $[1+\sum_ia_ip_i(\mu)]/D(\mu)$. This path uses neither the
tridiagonal elimination nor the tail recursion; the two are compared
directly in `test_angular.py`. It is also the fallback for a phase function
whose $\Gamma$ is not diagonal (@sec-method-choice).
:::

The distinction that matters for the final answer: **the coordinate-space
result uses a separate, exact first-order integral with the full HG phase
function** (@sec-coordinate-first), not the finite-$L$ $h^{(1)}$ above. So
the shipped result is
$$
K=K^{(0)}+K_{\mathrm{HG}}^{(1)}+K_L^{(\ge2)}.
$$
The finite-$L$ $h^{(1)}$ still matters — it is the right-hand side that
feeds $h^{(\ge2)}$ — but it is not itself reported. This is not the exact
solution of one finite-$L$ HG operator at fixed $L$: the first order is
resolved more precisely than that. As $L\to\infty$ the finite-$L$ solution
converges to the full HG answer either way. The exact composition of the
result is recorded in the output file's metadata (`GreenResult.save`).

## Spatial inversion {#sec-spatial}

Let $\nu=\widehat{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf s_0$. The angular integral over
$\widehat{\mathbf k}$ is done analytically through the spherical Bessel
function $j_l$:
$$
\boxed{
\tilde K^{(\ge2)}(r,\nu,\omega)=
\frac1{2\pi^2}\sum_{l=0}^{J}
i^l\sqrt{\frac{2l+1}{2}}P_l(\nu)
\int_0^\infty k^2j_l(kr)\,h_l^{(\ge2)}(k,\omega)\,\mathrm dk.
}
$$
$J$, the **spatial** angular degree, is independent of $L$: the
tridiagonal solve stops at $N=L$, and coefficients above $L$ are continued
up to $J$ by the exact free-tail ratios of @sec-matrix's closing callout —
the linear system never grows with $J$. For an isotropic source only $l=0$ survives,
with an extra factor $1/\sqrt2$.

The radial integral is a composite Gauss quadrature up to `k_max_per_m`;
with `taper=true` the weight is smoothly reduced over the second half of
the interval. This changes the numerical value of the integral — cutoff and
edge taper both need their own convergence scan, and so does $J$: a
spherical-Bessel sum needs roughly $J\gtrsim k_{\max}\cdot r$ multipole
terms to represent a function localized at radius $r$, a constraint
independent of $L$ or $g$ (@sec-bgvd-water works through a case where this,
not $L$, was the binding constraint). There is no 3-D FFT and no spatial
grid in $x,y,z$ anywhere in this path (`SolverSettings.quadrature`,
`PointGreenSolver.solve`). Within one call, frequencies are processed one
at a time; after the angular coefficients at a given frequency are found,
they are contracted against every requested observation point and
discarded. Only the resulting spectra are kept — there is no cache reused
between independent `solve` calls in this first release, though observation
points passed to the *same* call already share the angular solve
(@sec-bgvd-caching measures the resulting speedup directly).

Profiling a representative solve (`examples/point-green.toml`'s settings, a
single point, 241 frequencies) shows the tridiagonal solve itself is cheap;
almost all the wall time — about 70% in that configuration — is spent in
`_free_moments_and_ratios`'s own backward recursion for the free-tail
ratio $r_N$ (@sec-matrix's closing callout), whose iteration count is set by the
*slowest-decaying* $k$-node in the batch (the smallest $k$, near $k\to0$)
rather than by $N$ itself, and can run to several times $N$ as a result.
This is a real, measured cost, not a hypothetical one; it is not yet
addressed in this delivery.

## First order in coordinate space {#sec-coordinate-first}

For a directed photon, let $s=vt$, $r=|\mathbf r|$,
$\nu=\widehat{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf s_0<1$. The only possible scattering
point lies on the initial ray:
$$
a=\frac{s^2-r^2}{2(s-r\nu)},\qquad b=s-a,\qquad
\cos\theta=\frac{r\nu-a}{b},
$$
with $a$ the distance to the scattering point and $b$ the distance from
there to the detector. For $t>r/v$,
$$
\boxed{
K^{(1)}(t)=\frac{\mu_sv\,p_{\mathrm{HG}}(\cos\theta)\,e^{-\mu_ss-\mu_as}}
{b(s-r\nu)}.
}
$$
For $t<r/v$ the response is zero.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where this comes from"}
The formula is obtained by integrating
$\mu_sp(\cos\theta)e^{-\mu_t(a+b)}b^{-2}\delta(t-(a+b)/v)\,\mathrm da$,
keeping the Jacobian $\mathrm dt/\mathrm da=(1-\cos\theta)/v$. Its charge is
checked independently by integrating directly over $a$. For an isotropic
source and isotropic scattering ($g=0$), an independent closed form is
available as a cross-check:
$$
K^{(1)}(r,t)=\frac{\mu_s}{4\pi rt}e^{-\mu_tvt}
\ln\frac{vt+r}{vt-r},\qquad t>r/v.
$$
For an isotropic source at general $g\ne0$, a one-dimensional quadrature
over the ellipsoid $a+b=vt$ is used instead, after the substitution
$a=(vt/2)(1+\tanh y)$, which removes the $1/(ab)$ factor from the
integration measure. See `single_scattering_rate`, `single_spectrum`,
`single_bins`.
:::

## Charge and the time signal {#sec-charge}

The charge is $Q=\tilde K(0)$. In a bin centered at $t_b$ with width
$\Delta t_b$, the $\ge2$-scattering contribution is
$$
N_b^{(\ge2)}\simeq\frac1\pi\Re\sum_jw_j\,
\tilde K^{(\ge2)}(\omega_j)\,
e^{-\omega_j^2\sigma^2/2}\,
\Delta t_b\,\operatorname{sinc}(\omega_j\Delta t_b/2)\,
e^{-i\omega_jt_b},
$$
where $w_j$ are trapezoidal quadrature weights in $\omega$,
$\operatorname{sinc}x=\sin x/x$, and $\sigma$ is the width of an additional
Gaussian instrument response ($\sigma=0$: no smearing). Orders 0 and 1 are
instead integrated directly in physical time; at $\sigma>0$ their
convolution with the Gaussian is applied as a difference of normal CDFs at
the bin edges. @sec-histogram-binning explains why that split is necessary,
not just convenient.

`components` has shape `(frequency, observation, 3)`; the last axis is the
orders $0$, $1$, $\ge2$, not three specific collision counts. Time-domain
components have shape `(observation, bin, 3)`.

In the demonstration, 241 nodes on $[0,1.2]$ rad/ns give
$\Delta\omega=0.005$ rad/ns; the frequency-sum period is
$2\pi/\Delta\omega\simeq1256.6$ ns. Bins on an arbitrary window still use
the formula above, but periodic copies of the $\ge2$-scattering spectrum do
not vanish on their own — widening the window requires shrinking the
frequency step to compensate. Gaussian smearing produces its own tail
before $r/v$; the strict-causality check applies only at $\sigma=0$.

No negative value is ever clipped. The code returns the sum of negative
bins, the absolute unsmeared signal before the light front, and the
fraction of charge captured in the reported window (`readout.py`).

## Checks and limitations {#sec-checks}

At $g=0$, with $A=\arctan(k/d_0)/k$ (and $A=1/d_0$ at $k=0$),
$$
\tilde K_{\mathrm{iso}}(k,\omega)=\frac{A}{1-\mu_sA},\qquad
\tilde K^{(\ge2)}_{\mathrm{iso}}=\frac{\mu_s^2A^3}{1-\mu_sA}.
$$
This closed form checks the full scattering series; its independent spatial
inversion in the test suite uses an infinite-sine QUADPACK quadrature. At
$k=0$ the full angular monopole is $1/(\mu_a-i\omega/v)$ for any $g$ — a
check that scattering conserves photon number, matching @eq-number-balance
of @sec-rte at the level of the transported spectrum.

Rotations, a time shift, linear scaling with photon number, several
detectors solved together, pure ballistic transport, HG normalization, and
reading a synthetic double of the private interface are checked
independently as well.

This first module has no independent Monte Carlo confirmation, no finite
OM sphere, and no error estimate that holds uniformly over all geometries.
Scans over $L,J,k,\omega$ need to be extended for any new regime of use —
@sec-bgvd-water discusses one such extension, to measured water optics at
$g=0.9$, and in particular shows that the spatial degree $J$, not the
scattering degree $L$, is what must track $k_{\max}\cdot r$: a demonstration
this book had originally missed at large radius.

## Sources {#sec-sources}

The resolvent math and Fourier conventions were checked against
`baikal-rte/src/baikal_rte/spectral.py`, `frequency.py`, and the
`10-adjoint-frequency` notes of the predecessor project. The tridiagonal
route here is a new implementation, specialized to a point isotropic
detector and checked against an independent dense solver. The bilinear
reciprocity argument of @sec-adjoint is the standard transport-theory
adjoint/importance construction; see e.g. Bell & Glasstone, *Nuclear
Reactor Theory* (1970), ch. 6, for the general form this chapter specializes.

Definitions of the special functions and recursions:
[NIST DLMF, Legendre functions](https://dlmf.nist.gov/14),
[NIST DLMF, recurrence relations](https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.9). The radial
inversion uses
[SciPy `spherical_jn`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.special.spherical_jn.html).
